about.page-2.page-title-1: A Virtual Canvas of Botanical Dreams
about.page-2.body-text-1:
Spolia botanique invites architecture students, along with a wider public, to compose a virtual canvas of botanical dreams woven into the streets and squares of contemporary cities. Through playful mobile applications and immersive experiences, the project fosters forms of collaboration on a global scale while opening a space for reflection on the botano-digital future of urban environments. It calls forth the latent vegetal life concealed within the mineral fabric of the city, sketching the horizon of a chlorophyll-infused future in which floral imagination begins to permeate both architecture and technological thought.

These experimental applications allow users, wherever they are in the world, to transform their immediate surroundings into a vegetal utopia and to explore it through augmented reality. Equipped with a smartphone, each participant can enter this expanded form of urban space through an “augmented botanical walk,” where physical and virtual environments converge, and where botanical life and digital systems become deeply entangled.

The project seeks to provide inhabitants with an intuitive means of shaping the urban imaginary of their own city. Within this perspective, the figure of the metropolitan resident is redefined through the dual lens of Homo Ludens and Homo Faber, the human who plays and the human who makes, as articulated in utopian thought. Urban space thus emerges as a field of creative action and playful exchange.
about.page-2.caption-below-1:
Anatomy of a protea,

about.page-3.body-text-1:
In architecture, spolia designates the reuse of fragments taken from existing buildings and reassembled within new constructions. Here, the term is extended into a botanical and virtual domain, where the vegetal world is captured through meticulous 3D scanning and reconstituted as digital matter. These virtual gardens, assembled piece by piece, become a new kind of resource, akin to brick or stone, through which the city is reimagined as an immersive and shared botanical environment.

The project was developed in partnership with the Domaine de Chaumont-sur-Loire, the École nationale supérieure d’architecture de Paris-Belleville, and the joint research unit AUSser. The school functioned as a laboratory for experimentation, engaging students in the process, while AUSser ensured the scientific dissemination and articulation of the results. The festival offered a singular terrain for gathering the vegetal material that underpins the project.
about.page-3.caption-below-1:
A hologram dahlia,

about.page-4.body-text-1:
In 2022, Comet Lab was selected as one of twenty winners invited to design a garden for the Festival International des Jardins, hosted by the Domaine de Chaumont-sur-Loire. In tandem with this project, we partnered with the Domaine to develop a second initiative: Spolia botanique. This project was designed as an artistic and digital intervention set within the festival gardens.

Since 1992, the Festival International des Jardins at Chaumont-sur-Loire has served as a premier global laboratory for contemporary garden design and landscape architecture. As a vital incubator for new ideas, the festival constantly revitalizes the art of gardening. It engages both the public and industry professionals by introducing unique plant varieties, innovative materials, and visionary concepts.
about.page-4.caption-below-1:
Castle of Chaumont-sur-Loire,
Centre-Val de Loire Region.
about.page-5.body-text-1:
The Jardin d'Eaurmus, designed for this festival, featured a pathway centered around a menhir-like fountain. This structure generated a series of vortices in the flow of water in order to re-energize it. Like the nineteen other temporary gardens, it was dismantled after six months to make way for new creations by the following year's winners.

To preserve these ephemeral works, we used 3D scanning to digitize selected segments, effectively building a three-dimensional botanical archive. These high-resolution scans capture the rich plant and mineral details with remarkable precision. We then integrated the resulting virtual fragments into the Festum Virtual application, allowing for an immersive exploration of these environments.

The Jardin d'Eaurmus,
Laureate of the International Garden Festival,
at the Domaine de Chaumont-sur-Loire in 2022.
about.page-6.body-text-1:
The Spolia botanique project explores the concept of digital craftsmanship within the field of architecture, viewed as a convergence of the artisanal age and the digital era. This approach aligns with contemporary theoretical frameworks such as postmodern medievalism, digital archaism, and the primitive future, as explored by thinkers like Régis Debray and Jacques Lucan, and by architects such as Sou Fujimoto and Toyo Ito.

This line of inquiry is also central to the doctoral research of Mete Kutlu, the project lead and a former resident artist of the Villa Medici. He developed these ideas in his article "A Trans-Temporal Inquiry in Architecture," published in Culture et Recherche (no. 141, 2020). The project serves as a significant case study within his dissertation, which he defended in November 2025.

Traditionally, architects design projects using small-scale representations, often working within a studio far from the construction site. Our augmented reality application changes this dynamic by enabling design directly on-site and at full scale. The architect becomes immersed in the environment they are creating, establishing a more immediate and embodied relationship with the context. This aligns the design process with the spatial and sensory reality of the site.

The use of augmented reality reactivates the intuitive, hands-on bond that the medieval master builder shared with the construction site. It reimagines the site as a collaborative space where artisans worked and invisible imaginaries intersected. This technological shift challenges the architectural paradigm established during the Italian Renaissance, where the architect moved their imagination onto paper through systematic and abstract drawings.

about.page-7.body-text-1: Comet Lab offers architecture students a mobile application that enables them to design botanical and virtual augmentations of urban spaces. Through this platform, we seek to explore the following questions:
about.page-7.questions-1:
How can immersive design be developed through augmented reality tools to conceive future habitats where physical and virtual spaces are seamlessly interwoven?

How can contemporary cities be transformed into utopian urban scenarios, enhanced by suspended virtual gardens?

How might we imagine a virtual extension of a physical building; for example, a new digital façade for a Haussmannian structure, or a botanical urban skin that is variable, adaptable, and customizable according to the desires of each inhabitant?
about.page-7.caption-below-1:
Neon breakers in the desert,
3D scan of echeveria,
Garden Route, South Africa.
about.page-8.body-text-1:
The experience of our immersive design application serves as a crucial intellectual exercise for anticipating how the architect's role and tools will evolve in the age of artificial intelligence. It requires thinking within a hybrid and unprecedented environment, situated at the threshold between the physical world and the virtual domain.

The primary challenge lies in the need for precise integration of virtual constructions with existing buildings and urban settings. This condition compels the architect to operate simultaneously across both realms, perceiving virtual space as a direct extension of the physical environment. Ultimately, the goal is to conceive of these two domains as a fluid and symbiotic continuum.
about.page-9.caption-below-1:
Presenting Spolia botanique,
Maison des Métallos, Paris.

ultraviolet-city.page-11.body-text-1:
The aim of this research is to examine and outline the foundations of a possible alliance between the botanical and the digital, while envisioning the potential such an alliance may hold for the design of future urban habitats.

As evidenced by the growing body of scientific literature on artificial life, neurobiology, and plant intelligence, we are currently re-examining and redefining fundamental concepts such as "intelligence" and "life." This research seeks to engage with and expand these contemporary currents of thought, including posthuman critique. This perspective integrates multiple forms of intelligence within a single, inclusive planetary ecology that encompasses vegetal, animal, human, and artificial forms.

The project also aims to deepen reflection on the development of new approaches of architectural and urban design. These approaches move beyond anthropocentric frameworks, instead relying on the balanced collaboration of artificial, plant, and animal forms of life.
ultraviolet-city.page-12.body-text-1: Our research in the field of botany focuses on the systems of communication, intelligence, and interspecies collaboration that often remain invisible and elusive. Through an experimental mapping of plant habitats as perceived within the entomological world, we aim to render these microscopic, subterranean, and airborne networks more tangible. Our goal is to highlight the reciprocity between species coexisting within a shared ecology.
ultraviolet-city.page-12.questions-1:
What does it feel like to be a peony flower?

How does a bee perceive the world?
ultraviolet-city.page-12.body-text-2: Addressing such questions requires, first, a study of the unique sensory capacities of specific plants and insects, their modes of existence, and the ways in which they experience space and time.
ultraviolet-city.page-13.body-text-1:
To facilitate the weaving of connections between urban space, the digital realm, and the vegetal world, we studied selected works of science fiction where plant life is fundamental to imagining the cities of the future, whether fantastical, utopian, or dystopian.

Within these works, authors envision new types of spaces where human and vegetal life converge. These narratives challenge the conventional divide between human and non-human worlds, questioning traditional taxonomic separations. As critiques of anthropocentric attitudes and certain transhumanist aspirations, these stories propose, for instance:
ultraviolet-city.page-13.styled-list-1:
• "Flower-cities" constructed from vegetal matter as the final refuge of civilization in a post-apocalyptic world;
  • Communication systems based entirely on pollen and pheromones;
  • Aromas capable of bending space-time and nectars that weave connections between distant cities;
  • Living houses that grow from seeds like flowers.
ultraviolet-city.page-14.body-text-1:
While technophile scenarios imagine the future city dweller as a cyborg, part human and part machine, these narratives of floral renaissance conceive of a chimeric being: half human and half plant.

These literary works serve as a vital source of inspiration for developing compelling urban scenarios. We also examine the representation of imaginary vegetal environments in science fiction cinema, seeking visual references to inform and enrich these explorations.
ultraviolet-city.page-15.caption-below-1: The Mystery of the Third Planet (1982) explores variations of scale and color that resonate with the visual strategies later used in Avatar to construct fantastical, extraterrestrial vegetal environments.
ultraviolet-city.page-16.caption-below-1: The vegetal cities and imaginary flora of the planet Pandora in Avatar (2009) feature bioluminescent plants that evoke ultraviolet photography of flowers. Their exaggerated proportions generate landscapes that appear both immersive and radically alien.
ultraviolet-city.page-17.caption-1:
Neo-Assyrian representations of terraced gardens, canals, aqueducts,
          and monuments. Drawings traced from bas-reliefs of wall panels,
          Nineveh (Iraq), circa 7th century BCE.
ultraviolet-city.page-17.body-text-1:
The legendary accounts of the Hanging Gardens of Babylon represent a historical and utopian model for our experimental conception of a fusion between the contemporary city and nature in the age of artificial intelligence. These narratives convey a timeless dream held since the earliest cities: the aspiration to merge the urban environment with the natural world.

These gardens embody a dual urban symbolism that is both nostalgic and forward-looking. On one hand, they evoke the traces of our original habitat, reflecting the condition in which humans lived as hunter-gatherers within nature itself. This period gave rise to myths of the Garden of Eden, the tradition of Persian gardens, and broader imaginaries of a floral Paradise.
ultraviolet-city.page-18.body-text-1:
On the other hand, these gardens represent the technological capacity of urban society to shape its natural and cultural environments by materializing its urban reveries. Complex irrigation systems, large-scale water-lifting mechanisms, extensive networks of canals and aqueducts, and advanced construction techniques such as fired brick all contributed to this achievement. In this way, the Babylonians realized the dream of a garden-city through the constructive and urban possibilities afforded by their technologies.

These narratives provide a design model in which technology, nature, and the city are inextricably intertwined. Our aim is to reactivate this ancient vision through contemporary digital tools, replacing Babylonian hydraulic networks with networks of Wi-Fi, algorithms, and pixels to revive a holistic urban vision.
ultraviolet-city.page-18.pull-quote-1: To rethink the Hanging Gardens of Babylon in the age of artificial intelligence, to adapt them to contemporary cities, and to weave a planetary network of suspended gardens.
ultraviolet-city.page-19.page-title-1: Through the Eyes of a Bee
ultraviolet-city.page-19.body-text-1:
Artistic reference: an immersive online experience designed by Marshmallow Laser Feast, based on the 3D scanning of a forest environment as part of their project In the Eyes of the Animal. The primary work consisted of a virtual reality experience set within an English forest, where a VR headset allowed participants to perceive the environment through the unique sensory worlds of different animals.

The accompanying online platform and the animated film released on YouTube extended the project's reach, ensuring the work could be shared more widely and preserved beyond the duration of the initial physical installation.
ultraviolet-city.page-20.caption-below-1:
Images of a floral bouquet within the human-visible spectrum, captured
        using a mechano-optical device that closely approximates the spatial
        resolution of bee vision. The first image shows a segment that could
        easily be mistaken for fragmented parts of a scene, while the second
        reveals how a holistic view discloses the true form and structure of the
        flowers. The third suggests the potential completion and processing of
        the image within the brain.
ultraviolet-city.page-20.body-text-1:
While humans readily perceive the Gestalt of a scene, it was long assumed that insects such as bees relied only on elementary visual cues. Recent research, however, demonstrates that bees favor global processing while retaining the ability to attend to local elements within complex visual environments.

A.G. Dyer and S.K. Williams, "Mechano-optical lens array to simulate insect vision photographically," Imaging Science Journal, vol. 53, 2005, pp. 209–213.
ultraviolet-city.page-21.caption-below-1:
Hypothetical images of an orchid flower as perceived by a bee. (a)
          Photograph of a single flower and (b) an inflorescence of Orchis
          caspia. The reconstructed images (c, d, e, f) display the quantum
          captures of the three types of bee photoreceptors in false color.
          Image (c) corresponds to the resolution of the camera, while (d), (e),
          and (f) show how the flower is projected onto the ommatidial lattice
          at distances of 4, 8, and 12 cm, respectively.
ultraviolet-city.page-21.caption-below-2:
After Vorobyev et al., Institut für Neurobiologie, Freie Universität
          Berlin, 1997.
ultraviolet-city.page-22.body-text-1:
One of our primary objectives during the digitization phase is to reveal the colors and forms of the fantastic worlds that coexist alongside our own. Through this lens, one might perceive the world from the perspective of an ant climbing the peduncle of a jasmine flower, or a bee gathering pollen from the stamens of a hibiscus. A blue petal that appears relatively uniform to human vision may thus unfold into a rolling landscape—an extraterrestrial topography marked by hundreds of tonal variations.

To this end, we combine macro photography with ultraviolet imaging to construct three-dimensional environments that simulate the sensory worlds of insects. At present, there are no existing examples of 3D digitization that integrate these two distinct approaches.
ultraviolet-city.page-23.body-text-1:
Through the use of specialized lenses, macro photography enables a dramatic shift in scale, bringing us closer to the perceptual viewpoint of the insect. Textures, patterns, reliefs, and color gradients that previously remained unseen begin to delineate a floral architecture and organic landscapes that are at once familiar and foreign, appearing as if they emerged from a fantastical or extraterrestrial world.

Ultraviolet photography further enhances the perceptual capacity of the human eye by utilizing UV illumination to access colors beyond the visible spectrum. Unlike humans, most insects are capable of perceiving ultraviolet light. Under these conditions, nectar acquires a fluorescent appearance, tracing patterns across petals that remain invisible to human sight and appearing as luminous landing guides for pollinating insects.

immersive-sketching.page-30.body-text-1:
We conducted two 3D digitization campaigns in the gardens of the château, the first in July and the second in September 2022. In addition to these primary missions, we carried out spontaneous scans in and around Paris as specific needs emerged throughout the project.

During the first campaign, we were able to capture gardens with a greater abundance of flowers than in September. However, the primary challenge we encountered was the heat. Capturing tens of thousands of photographs under high temperatures repeatedly caused our equipment to malfunction. Despite these conditions, we completed approximately fifty scans in total at the Domaine de Chaumont-sur-Loire.

We utilized PhotoCatch to generate 3D models from the collected photographs. Each image corresponds to a flower, generated by photogrammetric algorithms that translate 2D images into 3D models.
immersive-sketching.page-31.caption-below-1:
Generation of a 3D geometric model and a 2D image
for color values from a set of photos.
immersive-sketching.page-32.caption-below-1: Generation of the final model by assembling the image and the model.
immersive-sketching.page-33.caption-below-1:
Unfolded flowers, algorithmic mapping. Each square image corresponds to a scanned flower. They are generated by
          photogrammetric algorithms translating 2D images into 3D models.
immersive-sketching.page-57.caption-below-1:
An unfolded peony flower, algorithmic mapping of colors during 3D
          scanning.
immersive-sketching.page-58.caption-below-1: A close-up view of digitized lilies.
immersive-sketching.page-35.body-text-1: The models produced through photogrammetric scanning are refined and cleaned so that they appear as fragments of reality, isolated and shaped into virtual clones. Their geometries and textures are further optimized through compression algorithms to facilitate efficient visualization within augmented reality environments.
immersive-sketching.page-36.body-text-1: The next stage involved the creation of a catalog of the digitized gardens, organized according to their scales and the botanical classification of the flowers they contain. Through this process, we identified shared characteristics among the different gardens and grouped them according to botanical families:
immersive-sketching.page-37.body-text-1: Commonly known as the family of asters, daisies, composites, or sunflowers, most species within Asteraceae are herbaceous plants, whether annual, biennial, or perennial. Their defining characteristic lies in the presence of numerous small individual florets grouped together and held by protective involucral bracts within a capitulum. This family has a remarkably wide distribution, found on all continents except Antarctica.
immersive-sketching.page-38.body-text-1: An inflorescence is a cluster or grouping of flowers arranged along a stem, composed either of a main axis or a more complex branching structure. The flowers within an inflorescence develop according to specific reproductive patterns, allowing for lateral or central growth. Their bracts serve both to attract pollinators and to protect developing flowers.
immersive-sketching.page-41.body-text-1:
We produced a series of 3D collages by recomposing digitized fragments drawn from heterogeneous botanical realities. These assemblages are then deployed as immersive environments to be explored through augmented reality.

At this stage, we examined how these botanical scans, treated as spatial components, could enter into a design process more familiar to the architect, specifically one mediated through the computer. We developed a working method in which the intermediate phase of drawing takes place digitally, situated between the initial digitization and the final immersive experience.
immersive-sketching.page-42.body-text-1:
These necessary articulations led us away from BIM environments such as Autodesk Revit, which tend to align architecture with the domains of engineering, commerce, and standardization. Such platforms remain distant from the technical, theoretical, and artistic flexibility required for the discipline to renew itself in the age of artificial intelligence.

Our 3D collages, conceived as recycled virtual gardens, are produced using Cinema 4D, a tool widely employed in the digital arts. Once constructed, each garden is visualized and tested in augmented reality. Based on these tests, the model is subsequently modified on the computer, allowing for an iterative exchange between Cinema 4D and augmented reality that can be repeated as many times as necessary.
immersive-sketching.page-43.caption-below-1:
An imaginary garden, 3D collage, prepared for an augmented reality
          experience.
immersive-sketching.page-44.body-text-1:
Following these initial experiments, we explored how augmented reality could be used directly within the act of design itself. Our aim was to set aside the computer during the design phase and to compose our "garden spolia" in an immersive, spatial, and immediate manner using an iPad or iPhone.

One of the key concepts that emerged from this research and development process is that of the immersive sketch. While three-dimensional environments designed entirely in augmented reality can be highly effective and visually compelling, they still require computer-based refinement to achieve greater precision. These models do not constitute final outcomes; rather, they serve as initial spatial sketches that facilitate subsequent stages of design.

Augmented reality thus appears to offer a significant transformation of the traditional architectural sketch. These intuitive and rapidly produced drawings are no longer confined to the flat surface of paper, but instead unfold spatially, surrounding the designer and expanding the field of architectural imagination.
immersive-sketching.page-45.body-text-1:
At this stage, we utilized Reality Composer, the application developed by Apple for the design of immersive experiences. This tool allows us to import our components and reassemble them directly in augmented reality. Beyond standard operations such as scaling and rotation, it also enables animation, the addition of interactive behaviors, and the integration of sound.

Once the composition is established, it is imported into Cinema 4D, where it serves as a reference for the development of a more precise final model. This model is then visualized in augmented reality for testing, and, if necessary, further modifications are carried out in Cinema 4D.

In conclusion, augmented reality does not eliminate the role of the computer in the design process, but rather enriches it through the introduction of the immersive sketch. It establishes a dynamic back-and-forth between computer and tablet, creating a vital alternation between two-dimensional representation and spatial, embodied design.
immersive-sketching.page-46.body-text-1: To develop the three applications, we used the development tools provided by Apple.
immersive-sketching.page-46.tech-value-2:
RealityKit / ARKit / SceneKit / UIKit / MetalKit / Foundation /
              QuickLook / SwiftUI / Model I/O
immersive-sketching.page-46.tech-app-desc-1:
To record user gestures, we rely on motion data captured by the
              device's gyroscope. Relative changes are computed in real time,
              allowing a flower to be positioned approximately 50 cm in front of
              the device.
immersive-sketching.page-46.tech-app-desc-2:
Visualization of 3D models without AR: SceneKit — Visualization in
              augmented reality: RealityKit

holo-botanics.page-68.body-text-1:
We explored various visual renderings to reveal both the variegated colors of vegetal life and the geometric forms of their new virtual existence. The objective was to design a visual effect that merges the botanical with the virtual. The resulting approach projects floral holograms and constructs the imaginary of a virtual botany.

Cameras were positioned to simulate the perspectives of an ant or a butterfly. Different types of virtual lighting were animated to imagine fantastical nocturnal scenes or to transform a plant into the central figure of a dramatic composition.

ar-apps.page-48.body-text-1: Festum Virtual enables the immersive exploration of digitized gardens in augmented reality. Users can navigate the three-dimensional botanical archive, experiencing the festival gardens as both spatial and temporal records.
ar-apps.page-49.caption-below-1: Screenshots from the app: the scan list, the AR and 3D views.
ar-apps.page-50.body-text-1: Spolia Botanique offers immersive experiences within virtual gardens. These environments are created through the recycling and recomposition of gardens that we have previously digitized. To animate them, we integrated animal life and sound recordings captured in forest environments. Hummingbirds move through the air, while large butterflies rest upon the flowers. The application presents three distinct gardens:
ar-apps.page-50.garden-desc-1:
Provides an atmospheric augmentation of the immediate environment.
              One walks through drifting particles of flowers suspended in the
              air. This garden does not replace the surrounding physical space,
              but introduces a volumetric enrichment.
ar-apps.page-50.garden-desc-2:
Merges the physical environment with an imaginary architecture. It
              invites the exploration of virtual ruins where diverse flowers
              have found refuge and a renewed form of existence.
ar-apps.page-50.garden-desc-3:
Transports the user into a dense and elevated virtual forest.
              Here, the physical surroundings are replaced by an immersive
              botanical dream of abundant vegetation.
ar-apps.page-55.body-text-1:
Floral Tracer is an experimental tool for immersive design that translates bodily movement into virtual gardens. Imagine your body as a brush painting petunias, and space as a botanical canvas: your surroundings are transformed into a living vegetal dream.

Beyond its role as a professional design tool, the application offers a distinctive artistic experience accessible to all. Within this environment, participants are invited to perceive architecture through the movements it generates and to consider themselves as a vital source of vegetal life.

Join this experience of virtual botany and explore the relationship between the human body and hybrid spaces in which image and intelligence are spatialized.
ar-apps.page-56.body-text-1:
Users of the application can populate the streets around them with fantastical gardens. They have access to a series of base compositions created by students, derived from the digitizations conducted at the Garden Festival of Chaumont-sur-Loire. These festival gardens, virtually recycled by Comet Lab and reworked by architecture students, can in turn be reappropriated and recomposed by anyone wishing to construct a botanical utopia within their own city. In this way, we extend our principle of botanical spolia: the reuse of vegetal resources at a planetary scale.

Once a street has been transformed into a botanical utopia, the user can capture an image of their creation, which is then automatically uploaded to the application. Over time, these images form a map that reveals the progressive construction of a virtual botanical fabric spreading across cities worldwide. One might thus witness the emergence of the suspended gardens of Paris along Rue de Rivoli, those of Venice in Piazza San Marco, or those of Tokyo at Shibuya Crossing.

Accessible to all, this map becomes the interface for a new form of social exchange mediated through the vegetal imaginaries of urban space. Tracing a virtual botanosphere across global cities, it reveals a chlorophyll-infused vision of the city: one that is more inclusive, more egalitarian, and more holistic in its understanding of the relationship between urban life and nature.

The Dream of Echinacea in Your Living Room: An Atmospheric

ar-apps.page-101.img-caption-1:
Screenshot of a student who has placed a virtual flower in front of a
          group of students observing other flowers on the tablet, thereby
          creating and merging fragmentary spaces.
ar-apps.page-101.body-text-1:
We conducted our user experience study with a group of 14 Master's students from ENSA Paris-Belleville on March 18 and June 10, 2024. This cohort, aged 21 to 24, provided a balanced representation of both men and women.

The primary objective of the experiment was to explore the potential of "immersive design" for architecture students and to evaluate the effectiveness of our application, Floral Tracer, in facilitating this experience. We sought to determine if our tool could tangibly improve and enrich their creative workflows.

While our focus remained primarily on Floral Tracer, the two additional applications, Spolia Botanique and Festum Virtual, were also evaluated. This allowed us to measure the students' mental and physical adaptation to augmented environments in which physical and virtual spaces merge into a singular experience.
ar-apps.page-102.body-text-1:
The students were fully engaged from the outset, demonstrating a high level of involvement and a rapid capture of their attention. The interfaces of all three applications proved effective and intuitive, allowing for seamless navigation between different views. Furthermore, the instructions provided at the start of each session facilitated a smooth experimental flow that required no external intervention.

They perceived the hybrid design environment—woven by the application between physical and virtual realms—as a natural setting that encouraged exploration and curiosity. For the majority of students, the fusion of these spaces felt entirely intuitive, reaching a degree of fluid integration that exceeded our expectations. Previously, we had conducted tests with participants over the age of 50, where the tendency was to perceive the augmented environment on the screen as a traditional, flat image. For that demographic, it was often difficult to interpret the screen as a window into a three-dimensional place; they remained relatively static and required a significantly longer adaptation period.

In contrast, the students expressed that the virtual gardens were perceived as tangible and physical entities, comparable to real botanical environments. They would occasionally stop abruptly to avoid stepping on a virtual flower or colliding with a virtual tree, even while sometimes bumping into physical furniture in their pursuit of a specific digital composition. For these users, the environments were lived and experienced as authentically real.
ar-apps.page-102.img-caption-1: Students creating virtual gardens in the classroom
ar-apps.page-103.img-caption-1:
A student creating a coneflower garden around the tables in Floral
          Tracer.
ar-apps.page-103.body-text-1:
The applications performed reliably, operating without bugs or technical malfunctions throughout the study. To maintain peak performance, we intentionally omitted certain advanced features, such as occlusion. Currently, the application overlays 3D models on the camera feed without allowing physical elements, like a hand or foot, to appear in front of the digital objects. This limitation slightly reduces the immersive impact; for instance, one student noted that while walking over virtual plants, he could not see his feet on the virtual ground. While this feature could be integrated, it would require further optimization of the models to maintain stability.

The experiment took place in a standard classroom, where the applications demonstrated a sophisticated ability to recognize and map the physical environment. The virtual garden models were integrated into the space with high precision. We encountered no "model drift," a common issue in augmented reality caused by poor environmental detection. Instead, the applications provided consistent scene recognition, ensuring an intuitive and continuous design experience for every participant.
ar-apps.page-104.body-text-1:
Each student naturally possesses their preferred tools; some favor paper and pencil, while others lean toward design software. Traditionally, these two groups are perceived as opposites in terms of their approaches, styles, and underlying schools of thought. However, while using our application, all students—regardless of their prior preferences—remained fully engaged and at ease. They reported that, much like with traditional sketching, their hands were directly involved in the design process, but with the vital advantage of creating directly within a three-dimensional environment rather than being restricted to two-dimensional representation.

The ability to generate 3D environments at their fingertips through various bodily gestures was crucial to the application's appeal across this diverse cohort. Participants indicated that this approach allowed them to transcend the conventional opposition between digital enthusiasts and proponents of classical methods. When the virtual image becomes spatialized and tangible, the application succeeds in merging the paradigms of artisanal and digital design: reconciling the hand and the pixel, and establishing a direct, manual relationship with the virtual universe.
ar-apps.page-104.img-caption-1:
A student drawing a floral tower with his gestures
and the resulting garden
ar-apps.page-105.body-text-1: A key factor in the students' interest lay in the application's integration of bodily movement, which transformed a traditionally passive design process into a playful, kinesthetic experience. Instead of remaining seated at a desk—drawing on paper or a screen—the students walked, stretched, leaned, and navigated the classroom. This physical activity allowed them to develop an increased awareness of their immediate surroundings, constantly questioning its limits and potential. As their movements were instantaneously converted into virtual gardens integrated into the physical environment, they developed a perception of their body as an active agent in the creation of space.
ar-apps.page-106.body-text-1:
The students quickly adapted to these hybrid environments and began to produce designs that leverage the unique characteristics of immersive design, distinguishing it from conventional 3D modeling on a computer.

By creating their designs directly within the image captured by the camera, the students utilized a canvas that was not the abstract, blank surface of a page, but a site animated by people and events. As a result, their creations showed a stronger connection with the activities taking place in the classroom and with the subtle details of the furniture and walls.

The students' creations were further distinguished by a specific volumetric plasticity. The gardens were not designed and generated in 2D, plan by plan; instead, they were the result of an instantaneous, three-dimensional creativity. They occupied not only the flat planes of the classroom, such as the floor and walls, but also the full volume of the room. The air—situated between the walls and often left as a white void on a traditional architectural plan—became a place that could host a variety of shapes and colors. It served as the direct medium of design rather than a consequential, unconsidered space assumed to be empty. These gardens were clearly not derived from plans and sections, but rather from depth and height: from the thickness of the space and the spatial paradigm that the image traversed.
ar-apps.page-106.img-caption-1:
A floral arch drawn by a student around me while explaining the
          exercise.
ar-apps.page-107.body-text-1: The designs also demonstrated that the virtual space with which we extend our physical reality does not necessarily have to be Newtonian or Euclidean. It is a realm where traditional laws of physics, such as gravity, can be entirely abandoned. In this way, a fantastic and unusual reality becomes an integral part of daily life in a tangible and interactive manner. The conventional perception of space and time becomes fundamentally invalid, even within the most mundane activities. The application proved that this new spatial paradigm requires tools that prepare students for such a shift, allowing them to design space in a more fluid and malleable manner. By embracing this freedom, the designer moves beyond the rigid constraints of the physical world toward a more speculative and liberated architectural practice.
ar-apps.page-108.body-text-1:
Our user experience test demonstrated that the application is more than a design aid; it serves as a catalyst for creative debate regarding architecture in the era of the climate crisis and artificial intelligence. Ultimately, the experiment prompted students to question fundamental aspects of architectural education and the design process. While proving their potential as generative tools, our applications enabled students to rethink architecture in relation to technology and nature. They were encouraged to reconsider the role of the body and the senses in space, moving beyond traditional oppositions such as virtual versus physical, nature versus technology, or body versus architecture.

The final discussion addressed a wide range of topics related to architectural design, including sensory and chromatic approaches, plant philosophies, new materialism, and "digital crafts." Students also examined the various design processes and teaching methods practiced in schools across France and abroad, enriching the debate with their international experiences and knowledge of diverse art, design, and fashion institutions. Ultimately, the experiment fostered an interdisciplinary and collaborative dialogue on the future of contemporary architecture.
ar-apps.page-109.img-caption-1: A student exploring an immersive forest
ar-apps.page-109.body-text-1:
The students had not previously encountered the concept of "immersive design" or experienced such a methodology. The applications we proposed were fundamentally distinct from any tools they had utilized during their studies at ENSA Paris-Belleville. Consequently, the experiment had an emancipatory and inspiring effect on the participants. They expressed that the application offered a new creative perspective for perceiving architectural space and the human body, inviting them to imagine novel compositions and sensations within the discipline.

Beyond the specific immersive design process we proposed, the experience encouraged them to develop more personalized methods and to reappropriate conventional design tools in experimental ways. This shift empowered them to cultivate more innovative architectural projects that challenge standard practices.
ar-apps.page-110.body-text-1: The students demonstrated a profound interest in this active, kinesthetic design process. We are observing a growing trend among our students toward practices involving manual labor and direct human interaction, such as the artisanal traditions of carpentry and masonry. This interest extends to creative environments like studios, construction sites, workshops, and fablabs; our application appeared to directly address these evolving needs.
ar-apps.page-110.body-text-2: The students also inquired about the possibility of exporting their models to a computer for further refinement. This functionality is already integrated into the application, and the participants found it highly advantageous to incorporate this innovative tool into more conventional architectural workflows.
ar-apps.page-111.body-text-1: We observed varying levels of immersion, distinct degrees of adaptation, and unique expectations shaped by the tools each student had already mastered, as well as the specific subjects they prioritize in their work. The feedback revealed that the application interacted dynamically with these diverse methods while offering fresh opportunities to question fundamental aspects of architectural design.
ar-apps.page-111.body-text-2: Working on floral patterns in Neapolitan earthenware, Jérémie realized that the flowers are consistently positioned at the same angle, parallel to the ground, regardless of the angle at which the phone is held. He noted that rotating the flowers in accordance with hand movement could significantly increase immersion. However, he also observed that Floral Tracer fundamentally alters the design process, allowing for a deeper interrogation of scale, the body, perception, material, and color.
ar-apps.page-111.body-text-3: Working on innovative forms of urbanism in the suburbs of Seoul, Doriann adopted the application with remarkable speed and began drawing gardens almost immediately. He remarked several times that the virtual gardens appeared so "present" that he almost tripped over a virtual stone or altered his path to avoid one. He also highlighted the positive impact of the app on the heightened perception of space and materials.
ar-apps.page-111.body-text-4: Working on sensory experiences in Stockholm, Julie expressed a slight lack of immersion and realism regarding the ground plane. Focusing on "promenades" in her research, she reported that the virtual ground is not visualized under the user’s feet, but rather appears layered on top of them. Despite this, she appreciated how the tool allows for a radical reconsideration of the interactions between the body and space, and how material and color influence sensory perception.
ar-apps.page-111.body-text-5: Working on precarious Indian habitats, Mathilde required additional time to accept the screen image as a three-dimensional environment. Unlike students who primarily work on computers, Mathilde—who favors hand drawing—initially needed more time to view the mobile phone as a window opening onto a hybrid world, moving within the space rather than observing it from a fixed position. Nevertheless, she recognized that the application opens new perspectives regarding spatial design and the nuanced understanding of scales and materials.
ar-apps.page-92.body-text-1: We successfully achieved all the objectives defined at the proposal stage.
ar-apps.page-92.label-1: In terms of research, we examined:
ar-apps.page-92.styled-list-1:
• Diverse methods for integrating augmented reality into architectural project methodologies and established design processes.
  • The inherent potentials and challenges associated with an immersive approach.
  • Distinct modes of spatial augmentation.
  • The resulting effects on spatial perception.
ar-apps.page-92.label-2: In terms of creation, we developed:
ar-apps.page-92.styled-list-2:
• An application serving as a digital extension of the Festival.
  • A specialized botanical immersion application.
  • A playful, kinesthetic immersive design application.
ar-apps.page-92.styled-list-3:
• An animation presenting the core project concept.
  • An immersive animation designed as a standalone exhibition piece.
ar-apps.page-93.body-text-1: We developed two application models within the project:
ar-apps.page-93.body-text-2: Both models rely on a shared set of basic components:
ar-apps.page-93.body-text-3: These foundational elements are combined with different 3D components to create two distinct augmented reality experiences, opening up two complementary paths for replication.
ar-apps.page-94.body-text-1:
This model enables the exploration of places or objects through two distinct modes: standard 3D and augmented reality. It provides a versatile framework for both interactive 3D viewing and context-aware AR visualization.

The system is particularly suited for the design of exhibitions, immersive museums, or virtual archives for diverse 3D datasets. Furthermore, it serves as a powerful research tool for scholars in the digital humanities. For instance, a researcher studying the remains of Pompeii could digitize artifacts in 3D rather than relying on traditional photography, later examining them within an immersive environment as if physically present.

Initially developed for the Festum Virtual application, this model has already been successfully integrated into Spolia Botanique, demonstrating its adaptability across different research and creative contexts.
ar-apps.page-95.body-text-1:
This model captures the precise position and orientation of the mobile device, calculating these fluctuations to generate a virtual trajectory onto which 3D objects are anchored.

By prioritizing the recording of bodily movement, this model serves as a foundation for projects centered on gesture and motion. Its applications extend across various disciplines, from dance and experimental artistic practice to educational tools designed to introduce complex topics to younger audiences through physical engagement.
ar-apps.page-96.body-text-1:
The three applications are intrinsically complementary, each offering a distinct and transformative experience that distinguishes them from existing market tools.

Their native compatibility with Apple Vision Pro provides a significant competitive advantage, positioning the project at the forefront of high-fidelity spatial computing.

Furthermore, the applications are unified within a coherent visual universe, reinforced by two specialized animations designed for broad dissemination across social media and immersive exhibition contexts.
ar-apps.page-97.body-text-1:
Initially, we intended to conduct experiments with student cohorts over a full semester or through intensive workshops, as collective engagement was essential to the project's methodology. Although ENSA Paris-Belleville was a partner, administrative constraints made it impossible to establish a formal course. Furthermore, the academic year was significantly disrupted by student strikes.

In response to these challenges, we welcomed two architecture students as interns. Their involvement allowed us to rigorously test various methods, tools, and approaches within the realm of immersive design. These experiences proved highly beneficial, contributing to the technical refinement of the project while providing deep insights into the opportunities and limitations of integrating augmented reality into architectural practice.
ar-apps.page-98.body-text-1: While all initial objectives were successfully achieved, we had originally envisioned a broader scope for the project. In particular, we aimed to integrate a mapping interface within the application to aggregate user-generated botanical transformations of urban spaces—effectively creating a form of botanical communication unfolding within augmented space. However, this feature could not be implemented during this phase due to technical compatibility conflicts between the various development tools.
ar-apps.page-99.styled-list-1:
• Securing strategic partnerships and funding to extend development, with a specific focus on the cartographic exchange system.
  • Doctoral dissemination and the academic valorization of research findings.
  • Direct integration into architectural pedagogy and education.
  • Collaborations with specialized institutions such as the École Nationale Supérieure de Paysage, horticultural schools (e.g., École du Breuil, Institut National d'Horticulture et de Paysage), landscape and architecture schools (e.g., ENSAP Bordeaux, ENSAP Lille), and landscape engineering programs.
  • Broad dissemination across digital platforms, social networks, and architectural journals.
  • Active participation in international design competitions.
  • Exploration of potential exhibition opportunities and immersive installations.
